rsonar in practice

Measuring and improving R code quality, step by step

Damien Dotta

What is rsonar?

rsonar is the R equivalent of SonarQube: it centralizes R code quality measurement into a single, interactive report.

Tool Role
lintr Static analysis — bugs, style, complexity
styler Code formatting
covr Test coverage
goodpractice Packaging best practices

SonarQube vocabulary: issues, Coverage, Quality Gate.

SQALE: quantifying technical debt

SQALE = Software Quality Assessment based on Lifecycle Expectations.

It is the method popularized by SonarQube — and adopted by rsonar — to turn code defects into an estimated cost, expressed in minutes.

Four key concepts:

  1. The penalty per issue (minutes)
  2. The debt ratio (%)
  3. The SQALE rating (grade from A to E)
  4. The method for calculating the estimated cost

The penalty per issue

Each issue has a remediation cost: the estimated time to fix it, in minutes.

Issue Default penalty
lintr error 30 min
lintr warning 10 min
Style violation 2 min
Badly formatted file (styler) 5 min
goodpractice failure 20 min
Missing coverage point 5 min / point

Total debt = the sum of these penalties.

The debt ratio

Total debt is compared to a reference effort:

ratio = D_total / (files × 30 min)
  • D_total: sum of the penalties for all issues
  • files × 30 min: estimated effort to develop the files

The quality score is derived from it:

score = 100 × (1 - min(1, ratio))

The SQALE rating (A → E)

The ratio is converted into a maintainability grade:

Ratio Grade Meaning
< 5 % A Excellent
5 – 10 % B Good
10 – 20 % C Acceptable
20 – 50 % D Poor
> 50 % E Critical

The estimated cost: the method

  1. Count the issues (errors, warnings, style, coverage, goodpractice)
  2. Sum their penalties → total debt in minutes
  3. Divide by the reference effort → debt ratio
  4. Convert the ratio into a SQALE grade (A → E)

Reference effort: SonarQube → lines of code × 30 min; rsonar → files × 30 min.

Example: 2 errors + 2 warnings + 5 style = 90 min, compared to 300 min (10 files) → 30 % ratio → grade D.

The plan: measure, improve, measure

A loop approach, using a running example:

  1. Start from problematic code
  2. Measure quality with rsonar (score, grade, debt)
  3. Improve the code step by step
  4. Re-measure and watch the grade go up

Version 2 — Refactor/document

Manual improvements:

  • rename Part_SAU → calculer_part_sau and SAU_HA → sau_ha (snake_case)
  • replace SAU_HA == NA → is.na() and class() == "numeric" → is.numeric()
  • remove the stray for (i in 1:length(...)) print(i) loop
  • fix the syntax error print("Done" and return to the implicit return

Version 2 — Refactor/document

#' Calculate the Useful Agricultural Area (SAU) share
#'
#' @param sau_ha Numeric or numeric vector. The SAU in hectares.
#' @param surface_totale Numeric or numeric vector. The total surface in ha.
#'
#' @return The SAU share as a percentage.
#' @export
calculer_part_sau <- function(sau_ha = 80, surface_totale = 100) {
  if (is.null(sau_ha) || is.null(surface_totale)) {
    return(NULL)
  }

  if (any(is.na(sau_ha)) || any(is.na(surface_totale))) {
    return(NULL)
  }

  if (any(sau_ha < 0) || any(surface_totale <= 0)) {
    stop("Surfaces must be positive and the total surface must be > 0.")
  }

  res <- (sau_ha / surface_totale) * 100

  if (any(res > 100)) {
    warning("At least one SAU value exceeds the total surface.")
  }

  return(res)
}

Version 3 — Add tests

tests/testthat/test-calculer-part-sau.R:

library(testthat)

test_that("calculer_part_sau computes the SAU share on a vector", {
  res <- calculer_part_sau(sau_ha = c(80, 120), surface_totale = 200)

  expect_equal(res, c(40, 60))
})

test_that("calculer_part_sau applies the default values", {
  res <- calculer_part_sau()

  expect_equal(res, 80)
})

Version 3 — Add tests (1/2)

res <- sonar_analyse(".",include_coverage = FALSE)

Version 3 — Add tests (2/2)

res <- sonar_analyse(".")

Why does the score drop to 0 %?

sonar_analyse(".") without include_coverage = FALSE measures coverage as soon as a tests/ folder exists. Here it is only 7 %: only one function is tested among the 10 scripts.

The coverage penalty then applies:

(80 − 7) × 5 = 365 min

This penalty alone exceeds the reference effort (11 files × 30 = 330 min):

ratio = debt / 330 ≥ 1
score = 100 × (1 − 1) = 0 %

→ Score 0 % · Grade E. It is the global project coverage that matters, not that of a single file.

Version 4 - Complete repository with tests and high coverage

  • See this repository to get a complete R project with tests and very high coverage.

The progression at a glance

Step Action Score Grade Coverage
0 Initial code 0 % E 0 %
1 Auto style (sonar_fix) 0 % E 0 %
2 Refactoring + docs 49 % E 0 %
3 Tests added without penalty 50 % D 0 %
3 Tests added with penalty 0 % E 7 %
4 Complete repository 98 % A 100 %

Each improvement raises the score and lowers the debt.

About coverage

Why does coverage only change at step 3?

Coverage is only measured when tests exist. Before (steps 0 to 2), it is 0 % and generates no penalty. At step 3, measuring coverage (7 %) triggers the penalty (80 − 7) × 5 = 365 min, which drops the score back to 0 %.

⚠️ To avoid this, you must cover the entire project (coverage ≥ 80 %), not a single function. Otherwise, it is the global coverage that drives the score down.

Going further: automate the fixes

The rsonar package can be integrated into a CI/CD pipeline to automate quality measurement and code reformatting. See this repository

Result: no more need to reformat code by hand before committing, nor to go back and forth in code review over simple style questions. A developer triggers the job, and a ready-made MR arrives with the formatting diff and all that’s left is to review and merge it.

CI pipeline example (GitLab)

  • See this repository

Minimal excerpt from .gitlab-ci.yml:

stages: [quality, autofix]

rsonar-check:
  stage: quality
  script: R -e "sonar_analyse('.'); export_junit()"

rsonar-fix:
  stage: autofix
  when: manual
  script: R -e "sonar_fix('.', create_mr = TRUE)"

Track the evolution over time

# Compare two analyses (before / after)
sonar_diff(res_v3, res_v0)

# Store scores over time to track the trend
sonar_trend(res, file = "rsonar-history.json")
  • sonar_diff(): new issues, fixed issues
  • sonar_trend(): evolution curve of the grade

Export the results (CI)

export_junit(res, "junit-results.xml")      # GitLab/Jenkins
export_sarif(res, "results.sarif")          # GitHub Code Scanning
export_sonar_json(res, "sonar-issues.json") # SonarQube

Standard formats: JUnit XML, SARIF 2.1.0, SonarQube Generic Issue Import.

Key takeaways

rsonar = measure, fix, secure:

  • Locally: quality_score() and debt_index() for immediate feedback
  • In depth: sonar_analyse() + sonar_report() + sonar_hotspots()
  • Over time: sonar_diff() / sonar_trend() to see the grade improve
  • In CI: quality_gate() + exports + sonar_fix(create_mr = TRUE)

Documentation: ddotta.github.io/rsonar · CI/CD integration
